title: Med Spa Loyalty Program: Earn Rates, Point Value and Expiry
summary: Med spa loyalty program setup: pick an earn rate and point value that match your margins, choose per-visit or per-dollar earning, and set expiry rules.
body_markdown:
## What a Med Spa Loyalty Program Should Reward


A med spa loyalty program should reward the behavior you want more of: an extra visit between injectable appointments, a retail purchase, a skin treatment added to a toxin visit. It should not pay patients for things they would do anyway, like returning for their regular 12-week toxin appointment at full price.


Start with one sentence that names the behavior. "We want facial patients to come every six weeks instead of every ten" is a program. "We want to reward loyalty" is a cost. In the clinics that ask us about loyalty points, the vague version is the one that ends up as a blanket discount nobody notices.


The guides that rank for this topic mostly describe two models. The[American Med Spa Association's loyalty program article](https://americanmedspa.org/blog/build-loyal-med-spa-clients-with-a-loyalty-program) compares a paid VIP club with a free points program at one point per dollar. Vendor guides add tiers and KPIs. Few of them show the conversion math or say what happens to the points nobody redeems, and those two gaps cause most of the setup questions we see.


## Loyalty Points vs Memberships vs Manufacturer Rewards


A loyalty program, a membership and a manufacturer rewards program are three separate things, and patients will confuse them if you do. A membership charges a recurring fee for a set of benefits. A loyalty program has no fee and pays back a share of visits or spend. A manufacturer program, such as[Allē from Allergan Aesthetics](https://news.abbvie.com/2024-01-23-Alle-by-Allergan-Aesthetics-is-the-Leading-Aesthetics-Loyalty-Rewards-Program-in-the-U-S) , is run by the brand, and you do not set its rules.


Model Patient pays to join Who sets the rules Best for


Membership Yes, monthly or yearly Your clinic Patients who visit monthly


Loyalty points No Your clinic Occasional patients you want back sooner


Manufacturer rewards No The manufacturer Brand-name injectables and partner treatments


One clinic we support had nineteen membership plans, several of them named "Loyalty Club," alongside a separate points program it was setting up. Its manager asked for a call because staff could not explain the difference to patients. Name things for what they are: call the paid plan a membership and the points "rewards" or "points." Our guide on[med spa membership pricing and retention](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-membership-pricing-retention) covers the recurring side in depth.


Patients already earning Allē points on toxin are a reason to point your own program somewhere else. Reward what the manufacturer does not: facials, retail, laser series and visit frequency.


## The Points Math: Earn Rate Times Point Value


The reward a patient receives is the earn rate multiplied by the dollar value of a point. Everything else, the 100-point thresholds and the gold tiers, is presentation. Work out the percentage of spend you are giving back before you choose any of the numbers patients see.


Program as written Point value What the patient gets back


1 point per $1 $0.01 $1 per $100 spent (1%)


1 point per $1, 500 points = $50 $0.10 $10 per $100 spent (10%)


10 points per $1 $0.01 $10 per $100 spent (10%)


10 points per visit, 100 points = $250 $2.50 $25 per visit, whatever the visit costs


10 points per visit $0.01 $0.10 per visit


The second row is the AmSpa example: 500 points for a $50 prize is a 10% reward. The same article notes that a product prize with a $50 perceived value may cost the spa about $25, which brings the real cost to around 5%. Redeeming points on your own services works the same way. A $50 reward used on a facial costs you the product and the provider's time, not $50.


The last two rows come from the same clinic's request. It wanted the fourth row and its software was set up for the fifth. Neither is wrong by itself, but a flat $25 per visit is a 25% rebate on a $100 visit and about 2% on a $1,200 one. If most of your visits are small, a per-visit reward gets expensive fast.


A practical rule: keep the value of one point fixed for the life of the program and change the earn rate instead. Our support team tells clinics to leave a point at one cent, because a cent is easy for staff to explain and hard to get wrong. As our[med spa discount policy guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-discount-policy) notes, a $100 gift at one cent per point is 10,000 points, not 100.


## Per Visit, Per Service or Per Dollar Earning


Choose per-dollar earning when you want the reward to scale with spend, per-service earning when you want to push specific treatments, and per-visit earning only if your visits cost about the same. Each model rewards a different behavior, and your software may support only some of them.


- **Per dollar.** Fair and easy to explain. One clinic planned to drop its membership discounts in January and replace them with 10 points per dollar spent. The catch is defining the dollar: before or after discounts, with or without tax and tip, and whether membership dues count.
- **Per service.** You set points on each service or product. This lets you put 300 points on a facial you want to grow and none on toxin. It also means a visit with two services earns twice, which surprised one owner who asked for "10 points per service" and meant once per visit.
- **Per visit.** Simple for patients and good for a punch-card feel. It ignores ticket size, so a quick follow-up earns the same as a full treatment unless you exclude free visits.


Write the earning rule as one sentence on the patient-facing terms. If staff cannot say it in one breath, patients will not understand it either.


## Set an Expiry Date for Every Kind of Point


Every point should have an expiry date. Points that never expire stay on your books forever and give the patient no reason to book this quarter rather than next year. A 12-month window from the date earned is a simple starting point and easy to state.


Separate earned points from goodwill points. One clinic wanted points it added by hand, for a delayed appointment or a complaint, to expire after 180 days, while purchase points kept the longer window. That is a sensible split. Goodwill points are a gesture, and a short window makes the gesture turn into a visit.


Tell patients the date. An expiry the patient never saw creates an angry call when the balance disappears. Show it on receipts or in the patient portal, and send a reminder a few weeks before a large balance expires. The text needs consent like any other marketing message, which our guide to[med spa text message consent](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-text-message-consent) covers.


## Redemption Rules: Minimums, Exclusions and Stacking


Redemption rules decide what the program costs, so write them before launch. Answer four questions in the terms:


1. **Minimum.** Can a patient spend 40 points, or only blocks of 100? A minimum makes the reward feel earned. If your software lets any balance be used, staff have to enforce the minimum.
2. **Exclusions.** Can points pay for toxin, gift cards, memberships or retail? Excluding gift cards stops points from being turned into cash value.
3. **Stacking.** Do points combine with a member discount or a promotion on the same ticket? One discount per ticket is the cleanest rule.
4. **Earning on redemption.** Does a visit paid with points earn new points? If it does, the reward compounds, so decide before launch.


One owner asked us to restrict points to certain services and categories. If your software cannot enforce an exclusion, it is a training rule, and training rules drift. Check what the system enforces before you print the terms.


## Unredeemed Points Are a Liability on Your Books


When a points program gives patients a real future discount, accrual accounting treats part of each sale as owed until the points are used or expire. Under ASC 606 this is called a material right.[PwC's guide to customer options](https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/pwc/accounting_guides/revenue_from_contrac/revenue_from_contrac_US/chapter_7_options_to_US/72customer_options_t_US.html) explains how revenue is allocated to the points based on their standalone selling price, reduced for the points expected never to be redeemed.[Deloitte's roadmap on breakage](https://dart.deloitte.com/USDART/home/codification/revenue/asc606-10/roadmap-revenue-recognition/chapter-8-step-5-determine-when/8-8-customers-unexercised-rights-breakage) covers how that unused share is recognized over time.


In practice, that has two consequences for a med spa. First, a mass gift is not free. One clinic asked to add points to every patient at once; another set up a $100 birthday points gift and stopped to ask what it would do to the P&L. Both create an obligation on day one, much of it held by patients who have not visited in years. Second, expiry is what lets the liability clear. The same thinking applies to packages and gift cards, which our guide to[med spa deferred revenue](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-deferred-revenue) walks through.


Some small clinics keep cash-basis books, where this works differently. Ask your accountant which method you use before the program launches, not at year-end.


## Keep Referral and Review Points Within the Rules


Points for referrals are allowed in many cash-pay settings but carry legal risk, and points for reviews break platform rules. Treat both carefully.


For referrals, a healthcare attorney writing for[AmSpa on patient reward programs](https://www.americanmedspa.org/news/patient-reward-programs-in-the-post-lockdown-medical-aesthetic-industry/) advises that referrals should not be the focus of a rewards program and that referral points should be set lower than the other ways to earn. The federal[Anti-Kickback Statute](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1320a-7b) applies where a federal health care program pays, and the same article notes that some state laws, including those in Texas and California, apply to all payers. Check your state before launch. Our[med spa referral program guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-referral-program) covers when the reward should be earned and how to track the referrer.


For reviews, the answer is simpler.[Google's contribution policy](https://support.google.com/contributionpolicy/answer/7400114) prohibits offering incentives such as discounts or free services in exchange for a review, and incentivized reviews can be removed. Leave reviews out of the program entirely.


## Launch Without Flooding the Points Ledger


Launch with new earning only, not a lump of free points for everyone. A launch bonus to patients seen in the last 12 months gets the program noticed without loading the books with points owed to people who have moved away.


Three launch details cause most of the clean-up work we see:


- **Migrated balances.** If you are switching systems, export point balances and expiry dates with everything else. Our guide to[what transfers in a med spa EMR migration](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-emr-migration-what-transfers) lists what to check.
- **Duplicate patient records.** Points split across two profiles for the same person show up as a balance dispute. Merge duplicates before launch and decide whether points can move between family members.
- **Staff permissions.** Decide who can add or remove points by hand, and require a note on every manual change.


Start with a one-page terms sheet: the earning rule, the value of a point, the expiry, the minimum and exclusions, and the right to change the program with notice. The AmSpa article suggests double points on slow days as a promotion lever once the basics run cleanly.


## How Decoda Health Runs Loyalty Points


Decoda Health sets loyalty earning on each service and product, so a clinic can put points on the treatments it wants to grow and none on others. The dollar value of a point is set once at the clinic level, and support recommends keeping the default of one cent. Patients redeem points as a payment method at checkout, and points are earned when a charge is settled, not on the portion paid with points.


Staff can add points to a patient by hand with their own expiry date, which covers the 180-day goodwill case above. Milestone rewards, such as a credit once a patient reaches 100 points, are built with a patient cohort and a promotion in[Decoda Health's growth tools](https://decodahealth.com/products/growth) , and promotions can also award bonus points.


Two limits are worth knowing before you design around them. Decoda Health does not calculate points from dollars spent today; earning is a fixed number per service or product, so a per-dollar program has to be approximated per item. It also does not restrict which services points can pay for, so exclusions are a front-desk rule. Points sit next to[memberships](https://decodahealth.com/products/memberships) ,[packages](https://decodahealth.com/products/packages) and[billing](https://decodahealth.com/products/billing) in the same system, so the liability and the redemption history are in one place.


## Measure Whether the Program Changes Visits


A loyalty program works if enrolled patients come back sooner or spend more than they did before, and the cost of the rewards is lower than the margin on those extra visits. Points issued is not the measure.


Track four numbers each quarter:


- Days between visits for patients who earned points, before and after launch
- Redemption rate: points redeemed divided by points issued
- Reward cost as a share of revenue from enrolled patients
- Outstanding points balance, the liability figure your accountant will ask for


A redemption rate near zero means patients do not know the program exists, or the rewards are out of reach. A very high rate with no change in visit frequency means you are paying patients for visits they would have made anyway. Our guides on[med spa KPI tracking](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-kpi-tracking) and[retention and rebooking](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-retention-and-rebooking) cover the visit-frequency side, and[Decoda Health analytics](https://decodahealth.com/products/analytics) reports revenue by patient cohort.


## Final Thoughts on Your Med Spa Loyalty Program


Decide the percentage you will give back, then pick an earn rate and point value that produce it. Choose whether points follow the visit, the service or the dollar. Put an expiry on every point, keep referral rewards small, leave reviews out, and launch with new earning instead of a giveaway. Review the four numbers after one quarter and change the earn rate, not the point value, if the program costs too much. ## Frequently Asked Questions


How many points per dollar should a med spa loyalty program give?


One point per dollar is a common starting rate, used in the American Med Spa Association's sample program, but the earn rate means nothing until you set what a point is worth. Multiply the two to get the share of spend you give back. One point per dollar at one cent per point returns 1%, while the same earn rate at ten cents per point returns 10%. Pick the return first, then the numbers.


Should med spa loyalty points expire?


Yes. Points that never expire stay on your books as an obligation indefinitely and give patients no reason to come back soon. A 12-month window for earned points is a simple starting point. Goodwill points that staff add by hand, such as a service-recovery gesture, can carry a shorter window like 180 days. Put the rule in the program terms and show the expiry date to the patient.


Is a loyalty program better than a membership for a med spa?


They do different jobs. A membership charges a recurring fee and gives predictable revenue, so it suits patients who come in monthly. A loyalty program has no fee and rewards visits or spend, so it suits occasional patients you want to see more often. Many med spas run both, but members should not also earn points on their membership dues, or the two discounts stack.


Can a med spa give loyalty points for referrals or reviews?


Referral points are possible but should be small, and your state's rules come first. Healthcare attorneys advise keeping referrals from being the focus of a rewards program, and the federal Anti-Kickback Statute applies wherever a federal health program pays. Do not give points for reviews. Google's policy bans incentives such as discounts or free services in exchange for a review.


Do unredeemed loyalty points count as a liability?


Under accrual accounting, usually yes. When points give the patient a material right to a future discount, part of the original sale is deferred until the points are redeemed or expire, with an estimate for points that will never be used. Clinics on cash-basis books handle it differently, so ask your accountant which method applies to you before launching.


Do Allē points replace a med spa's own loyalty program?


No. Allē is run by Allergan Aesthetics and rewards patients for that manufacturer's treatments, and you do not control its earn rates or expiry. Your own program can reward what Allē does not, such as facials, retail and visit frequency. Tell patients plainly which points are yours and which belong to the manufacturer.
